name: Dexpanthenol
lead: Dexpanthenol (also panthenol, provitamin B5) is the stable alcohol analog of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5). Pantothenic acid is a component of coenzyme A and is described as essential to normal epithelial function; topical dexpanthenol is used on skin because it penetrates well and reaches high local concentrations.[1] It appears in barrier-supporting and soothing skincare products, often as a humectant at concentrations of a few percent.

Research on topical dexpanthenol has centred on wound healing, skin irritation and radiation-related skin reactions rather than on cosmetic outcomes.[1][2][3] A 70th-anniversary review of its topical use and a 2020 review on wound healing summarize this literature.[4][5]
infobox: Vitamin B5 analog (alcohol of pantothenic acid)
Topical (creams, ointments, eye gels); also in parenteral B-vitamin preparations

paras: Dexpanthenol is used in moisturizers and ointments for dry or irritated skin and minor wounds.[1][4] A registered phase 2 study compared the moisturizing effect of two dexpanthenol formulations.[8]

Studies have tested dexpanthenol in radiation dermatitis; one randomized trial compared 0.5% dexpanthenol with 0.1% methylprednisolone in breast cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy.[3] Clinical practice guidelines on radiation reactions from the MASCC Skin Toxicity Study Group are among the literature that discusses such topical agents.[2] Registered trials have also examined it for skin rash from EGFR inhibitors, lip-corner cracks and dry eye.[9][10]
Pantothenic acid is a cofactor in enzyme-catalysed reactions of carbohydrate, fatty acid and protein metabolism, and topical dexpanthenol is converted to it in tissue.[1]

Human studies are mostly small and focus on wound healing and irritation. The radiation dermatitis trial compared dexpanthenol with a topical corticosteroid.[3] A phase 4 molecular-level study examined 5% dexpanthenol ointment on superficial injuries in 15 subjects.[7] Appearance outcomes such as skin texture or anti-aging have not been the main endpoints of the studies listed here.

card.summary: Vitamin B5 derivative in soothing, barrier-support skincare; studied mainly for wound healing and irritation.
card.note: Evidence is mostly for wound healing and irritated skin, not cosmetic appearance outcomes.

quick.overview:
Dexpanthenol is a form of vitamin B5 found in many moisturizers and ointments, usually marketed for soothing dry or irritated skin.

Research has looked mainly at wound healing and radiation-related skin reactions, with small trials.
quick.mechanism: It is converted to pantothenic acid, a part of coenzyme A that supports normal epithelial function, and is thought to act as a humectant on skin.[1]
quick.risks: Topical use is described as well tolerated in the reviews listed; this entry does not cover injected B-vitamin products.
